prompt.context: A client owns a large bank with many branches and wants to get out of the banking business. With $100M in losses, he hopes to find a new business to acquire, against which he can offset the losses (losses carry forward).
prompt.question: Recommend an acquisition candidate.

framework: Step 1 – Identify a well-performing company in an attractive industry that meets the client's financial objectives
The new company's net income within the next 15 years should be sufficient to cover the $100M in banking losses
Long-term attractiveness matters: once losses are written off, the client must be able to sell the new business at a good price if desired
Leverage existing bank capabilities (customer research expertise, geographical spread, etc.) when selecting the industry
Most start-ups are not viable given the significant profitability requirements — focus on established businesses
Step 2 – Assess whether the banking business has sufficient management and operational capabilities to run a diversified company
Ensure that the cost of complexity from running a diversified portfolio does not exceed the benefits of diversification

questions.prompt: What financial criteria must the acquisition target meet?
questions.guidance: The target's cumulative net income over the next 15 years must be large enough to absorb the $100M loss carry-forward from the banking business. This means the target needs consistent profitability, not a turnaround story. Candidates should quantify a minimum annual net income threshold (e.g., ~$7M/year over 15 years as a rough floor) and consider the time value of money if advanced.

math.setup: $100M losses to offset over 15 years; minimum required average annual net income
steps: $100M / 15 years ≈ $6.7M average annual net income minimum
Actual requirement may be higher to account for time value of money and desired return on acquisition price
math.answer: Roughly $7M+ average annual net income over 15 years as a baseline; higher if discounted

questions.prompt: What industry or company characteristics should the client look for?
questions.guidance: Use Porter's 5 Forces and 3 C's to evaluate industry attractiveness. Look for industries with high barriers to entry, low buyer/supplier power, limited substitutes, and low competitive rivalry. Leverage the bank's existing capabilities — customer research, geographic branch network, relationship management — as a competitive advantage in the new business. Avoid highly capital-intensive or regulated industries unless familiar.

questions.prompt: What internal capabilities must the client assess before proceeding?
questions.guidance: Step 2 of the framework: evaluate whether bank management has the skills to run a diversified company. Key dimensions include: management bandwidth and expertise in the new industry, ability to oversee a portfolio of distinct businesses, and whether the incremental complexity costs (management overhead, integration costs, distracted focus) outweigh diversification benefits.

brainstorming.prompt: What types of industries or businesses would be attractive acquisition candidates for the bank client?

categories.name: Leverage existing bank capabilities
ideas: Financial services adjacencies (insurance, asset management, leasing)
Businesses with large retail customer bases (similar to branch network)
Industries requiring strong geographic distribution networks

categories.name: Stable, profitable businesses
ideas: Franchise-based businesses with predictable cash flows

categories.name: Avoid
ideas: Highly regulated industries requiring new licensing

recommendation: Recommend acquiring an established, profitable company in a non-cyclical industry adjacent to financial services or leveraging the bank's geographic and customer-research capabilities
Target should have demonstrated consistent net income of at least ~$7M/year to offset $100M in losses within 15 years
Prioritize a business the bank's management team can credibly oversee without excessive complexity costs
risks: Management may lack expertise in the new industry, increasing execution risk
Diversification complexity costs could erode the financial benefit of the loss carry-forward
If the acquired business underperforms, the client loses both the tax benefit and the acquisition investment
Regulatory constraints on bank holding company structures may limit acquisition options
next_steps: Screen acquisition candidates using financial and industry attractiveness criteria
Conduct management capability assessment to confirm the client can run the new business
Engage M&A advisors to identify specific targets and negotiate valuation
Model out loss carry-forward utilization under conservative, base, and optimistic scenarios
